source_title: NIKE, Inc. Form 10-K, fiscal year ended May 31, 2022 (with fiscal 2023 first-quarter and full-year follow-on)
publisher_issuer: NIKE, Inc. (SEC Form 10-K and related results releases)
company_context: NIKE, Inc. is a global athletic footwear and apparel company. Through fiscal 2022 and into fiscal 2023, Nike carried elevated inventories driven by extended lead times and supply-chain disruption that pushed large volumes of product in-transit, later compounded by softer-than-expected demand that required markdowns to clear.
business_type: Global branded athletic footwear and apparel (wholesale and direct-to-consumer)
geography: Global (headquartered United States; significant North America, EMEA, Greater China, APLA segments)
time_period: Fiscal 2022 (ended May 31, 2022), fiscal 2023 Q1 (ended August 31, 2022), and fiscal 2023 (ended May 31, 2023)
macro_context: 2021-2023 global supply-chain disruption and extended ocean/logistics lead times, followed by a 2022 demand softening in discretionary goods and elevated promotional activity across apparel retail.
outcome_category: 8 - fast-growth/operational breakdown contained (elevated inventory and markdown pressure that is subsequently worked down)
evidence_summary: Nike ended fiscal 2022 (May 31, 2022) with inventories of $8,420 million (about $8.4 billion), up about 23 percent year over year, driven by elevated in-transit inventories from extended lead times amid supply-chain disruption, partially offset by strong consumer demand. The mismatch peaked in fiscal 2023 first quarter (ended August 31, 2022), when inventories reached about $9.7 billion, up 44 percent year over year, again driven by elevated in-transit inventory amid supply-chain volatility. By fiscal year-end 2023 (May 31, 2023) inventories were about $8.5 billion, roughly flat versus the prior year, and North America inventories had been reduced from $4,098 million (2022) to $3,806 million (2023), indicating the glut was actively worked down through markdowns and tighter buying. This is a documented inventory-forecasting/lead-time mismatch with quantified build-up and subsequent normalization.

source_backed_metrics.fy2022_ending_inventory_may_31_2022: $8,420 million (about $8.4 billion), up about 23 percent year over year
source_backed_metrics.fy2023_q1_inventory_aug_31_2022: approximately $9.7 billion, up 44 percent year over year
source_backed_metrics.fy2023_ending_inventory_may_31_2023: approximately $8.5 billion (roughly flat year over year)
source_backed_metrics.primary_cited_cause: elevated in-transit inventories from extended lead times and supply-chain disruption

owner_decision_context: Management attributed the build-up to in-transit inventory from supply-chain lead times rather than weak demand, and over fiscal 2023 prioritized clearing excess through markdowns and disciplined buying, especially in North America.
action_taken: Markdowns and promotional clearance plus tighter inventory buying through fiscal 2023 to normalize inventory levels, particularly in North America.
outcome_evidence: Inventory rose from $8.4 billion (FY2022) to a $9.7 billion peak (Q1 FY2023, +44 percent) then was worked back down to about $8.5 billion (flat) by FY2023 year-end, with North America inventory falling from $4,098 million to $3,806 million.
source_limitations: SEC EDGAR filing pages returned HTTP 403 on direct fetch; the inventory values, percentage changes, and cited causes were confirmed verbatim in Nike investor-relations, Business Wire, and SEC-indexed primary-domain search snippets rather than read in full filing text. The 44 percent peak and the $9.7 billion figure come from the fiscal 2023 first-quarter results release; the $8.4 billion and $8.5 billion year-end figures come from the fiscal 2022 and fiscal 2023 10-Ks respectively.

why_useful_for_opsiq: A large-cap inventory_forecasting_mismatch driven primarily by supply-chain lead times rather than demand failure, with a clear build-up-then-normalization trajectory. Useful for testing whether OpsIQ separates an in-transit/forecasting inventory problem from a demand or pricing-power problem, and for modeling adaptive re-evaluation across a KPI deterioration that is subsequently contained.
